summary: This memo defines part of the SNMP Management Information Base for managing multiple logical and physical entities handled by a single SNMP agent. It specifies version 4 of the Entity MIB and obsoletes version 3, published as RFC 4133.

eli5.summary: A big machine has many parts, like a car with an engine and wheels. This gives network tools a standard way to list and describe all the parts.

questions: snmp physical and logical entity management
what changed in entity mib version 4
subtitle: The standard SNMP table that lists a device's physical parts and the logical devices running on them.

tldr.problem: One SNMP agent can speak for several logical devices (bridges, repeaters, OSPF instances) inside one physical box, and managers had no standard way to list them or the hardware they run on.
tldr.mechanism: The Entity MIB defines tables for physical components arranged as a containment tree, tables for logical entities, and mapping tables that tie the two together. Version 4 adds a UUID object, an IANA-maintained list of physical classes and a smaller compliance profile.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes version 3 (RFC 4133). Managers get a common inventory model of chassis, modules, ports and the logical entities that use them.

today: RFC 6933 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2013. It obsoletes RFC 4133 (Entity MIB version 3), and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Problem: Many Entities, One Agent
sections.content:
RFC 6933 defines version 4 of the Entity MIB, a module of the SNMP Management Information Base. It is about one situation: a single SNMP agent that manages several instances of the same MIB module. The RFC gives three examples: several bridges in one device, several repeaters under one agent, and several OSPF backbone areas, each identified by the same area-id, inside one router.

In such a device there is an overall physical entity that houses everything the agent manages, and several logical entities inside it. Sometimes that physical entity is itself a compound of smaller ones, such as a stack of stackable hubs. A manager needs to know exactly which logical entities the agent handles so it can talk to the agent about a particular one.

The RFC says the context or community in the SNMP message can identify the logical entity, so there is no need for varbinds of several logical entities in one message.
sections.eli5: Imagine one big toy box that holds several different games. Before you play, you need a list of which games are inside. This MIB is that list.

sections.title: Key Terms: Entities, Naming Scopes and Containment
sections.content:
The RFC defines a handful of terms. A logical entity is something like a router, bridge or print-server, each represented by at most one instantiation of a particular set of MIB objects. A physical entity is an identifiable physical resource such as a port, backplane, sensor, daughter-card, power supply or the overall chassis. Which components appear in the table is an implementation-specific matter.

A naming scope is the set of information reachable through a single SNMP operation. For SNMPv1 it is identified by the value of entLogicalCommunity; for SNMPv3 the term "context" is used instead. A multi-scoped object has the same instance value meaning different information in different scopes, while a single-scoped object means the same thing in all of them.

Physical components form a containment tree. Following each entPhysicalContainedIn value upward until a value of zero gives the exact physical location of a component.
sections.eli5: Think of a doll that holds a smaller doll that holds a smaller doll. To say where one doll is, you list which doll it sits in, until you reach the biggest one.

sections.title: The Five Groups of Objects
sections.content:
The MIB has five groups. The entityPhysical group holds the entPhysicalTable, with one row per physical entity. It must always contain at least one row for an overall entity, which should have a class of stack(11), chassis(3) or module(9). Each row has an arbitrary small integer index, a description and type, and optionally the index of the entry that contains it.

The entityLogical group holds entLogicalTable, with a name, description and type for each logical entity plus the information needed to reach its MIB data, either by community name or by SNMPv3 context. An agent that represents a single logical entity, or several within one naming scope, may omit this group.

The entityMapping group has three tables. entLPMappingTable maps logical entities to the physical components that support them (many to many). entAliasMappingTable maps pairs of logical and physical indexes to object identifiers of resources in other MIB modules, such as interfaces or repeater ports. entPhysicalContainsTable lets a manager quickly find all children of a physical entity.

The entityGeneral group has one scalar, entLastChangeTime, the value of sysUpTime when any part of the Entity MIB configuration last changed. The entityNotifications group holds notifications about the status of the MIB instance.
sections.eli5: It is like a school directory with a list of rooms, a list of classes, a chart showing which class uses which room, and a note of when anything last changed.

sections.title: Identifying a Physical Component
sections.content:
Each row of entPhysicalTable carries descriptive and identifying objects. The usage examples show them in action: description, vendor type, containing entity, class, relative position, name, hardware, software and firmware revisions, serial number, manufacturer name, model name, alias, asset ID, a flag for field-replaceable units, manufacturing date and URIs.

Three strings are writable. entPhysicalAlias is a non-volatile identifier an NMS can assign, and an agent may generate it algorithmically. entPhysicalAssetID stores a user-specific asset identifier, and the RFC advises assigning it only to field-replaceable components to save non-volatile storage. entPhysicalSerialNum can be set by hand when the agent cannot detect serial numbers.

Version 3 added entPhysicalMfgDate and entPhysicalUris, which holds one or more URIs separated by white space, for example a CLEI URN such as URN:CLEI:D4CE18B7AA. Version 4 adds entPhysicalUUID, a read-only globally unique identifier in the format of RFC 4122. For compatibility with version 3 implementations, entPhysicalUris should also carry the UUID in URN form.
sections.eli5: Every part gets a name tag: what it is, who made it, its serial number, and a special one-of-a-kind ID that no other part in the world shares.

sections.title: What Version 4 Changes
sections.content:
Version 4 addresses requirements that came up after RFC 4133. The RFC lists three changes.

  • IANA-ENTITY-MIB. The PhysicalClass textual convention is deprecated and replaced by IANAPhysicalClass, maintained by IANA, so new classes can be added without reissuing this MIB module. The list now includes values such as energyObject(13) and battery(14).
  • UUIDs. A new UUIDorZero textual convention in the UUID-TC-MIB module, and the read-only entPhysicalUUID object.
  • Constrained devices. Two compliance statements: entity4Compliance for full compliance, and entity4CRCompliance for devices with constrained resources such as batteries, which need to support only entPhysicalClass, entPhysicalName and entPhysicalUUID.

The RFC also summarizes earlier changes: version 2 added the SNMPv3 context objects and revision, vendor and alias objects, and version 3 added the CPU class, the PhysicalIndexOrZero convention, and the manufacturing date and URI objects.
sections.eli5: The new version adds a unique serial-style ID for every part, a list of part types that can grow over time, and a lighter version for tiny gadgets that cannot keep a long list.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 4 walks through example devices. The first is a router with two slots, each holding a 3-port router/bridge module, with two logical OSPF instances and two logical bridges. The second covers repeaters. Auxiliary parts such as fans, sensors and empty slots are left out to keep the examples simple.

The third, added for energy management (EMAN), shows a router with 16 slots with line cards. It lists three components: a chassis (class chassis(3)), a slot inside it (container(5)) and a line card in that slot (module(9)). Each row includes both an entPhysicalUris URN and a matching entPhysicalUUID.
sections.eli5: The examples are like drawing a family tree of a real machine: the box, the shelf in the box, and the card on the shelf.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects are read-write, and the RFC says setting them without protection can hurt network operations. Misconfiguration or disclosure of entPhysicalSerialNum, entPhysicalAlias, entPhysicalAssetID and entPhysicalUris may reveal asset information, disturb management, or cause privacy issues if values can be used to track something personally identifying.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. They expose vendor, model and version details, the community names in entLogicalCommunity, and the network addresses and SNMP engine information in the logical entity table. The RFC says access to them should be controlled and values possibly encrypted in transit.

Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features. Those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy with the User-based Security Model and the AES cipher. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A list of every part of a machine is handy for repair people, but also for burglars. So only the right people should be allowed to read or change it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC creates the first version of the IANA-maintained IANA-ENTITY-MIB module. Every change to the IANAPhysicalClass list requires Expert Review.

The ENTITY-MIB module uses the object identifier { mib-2 47 }. IANA also allocated { mib-2 216 } to ianaEntityMIB and { mib-2 217 } to uuidTCMIB.
sections.eli5: A librarian keeps the official list of part types, and new types can be added only after a careful check.

items.label: other
items.desc: Not one of the other classes.

items.label: chassis
items.desc: The overall box; a typical top-level entity.

items.label: container
items.desc: For example a chassis slot or daughter-card holder.

items.label: module
items.desc: For example a plug-in card or daughter-card.

items.label: stack
items.desc: For example a stack of multiple chassis entities.
